canonical_statement: The study aimed to characterize clinical syndromes, management patterns, and predictors of mortality in invasive listeriosis over 45 years, with particular attention to long-term outcomes and adjunctive gentamicin.
Eligible cases were adults with laboratory-confirmed invasive Listeria monocytogenes infection identified from January 1, 1980 through December 31, 2024.

population.label: Adults with laboratory-confirmed invasive Listeria monocytogenes infection

canonical_statement: Cases were identified through microbiology laboratory records across Mayo Clinic Health System sites and reviewed retrospectively.
Invasive infection was defined by detection of Listeria monocytogenes from a normally sterile site by culture or a molecular method such as PCR.

Each case was assigned one predominant clinical syndrome: primary bloodstream infection, neurolisteriosis, pregnancy-associated infection, or another focal infection such as endovascular infection or peritonitis.

Immunocompromised status included malignancy, immunosuppressive therapy or chronic corticosteroids, solid-organ or hematologic transplantation, asplenia, or HIV; diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease alone were not classified as immunocompromising conditions.
The primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality, defined as death from any cause within 1 year of invasive listeriosis.

outcome.definition: Death from any cause within 1 year

canonical_statement: Secondary outcomes included 90-day mortality and residual neurological deficits among patients with neurolisteriosis.
Residual neurological deficits were defined as new or worsened neurologic abnormalities attributable to neurolisteriosis and present at discharge.

outcome.definition: New or worsened neurologic abnormality attributable to neurolisteriosis at discharge

canonical_statement: Because mortality events were limited, the investigators restricted Cox proportional-hazards analyses to univariate models to reduce overfitting.
The study received institutional review board approval with waiver of informed consent.
The cohort contained 50 adults with invasive listeriosis.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that immunocompromised host status and ICU-level illness at presentation were the strongest observed predictors of higher 1-year mortality.
The authors concluded that blood cultures remain critical for diagnosing neurolisteriosis and that CSF PCR can add diagnostic utility when cultures are negative.
The authors concluded that aminopenicillin-based therapy remained the cornerstone of treatment and that adjunctive gentamicin did not show a survival benefit in this cohort.
The authors called for larger multicenter prospective studies to clarify optimal therapy and improve risk stratification.
The authors described the retrospective, single-center nature of the study and small sample size with few mortality events as limiting generalizability and statistical power.
Most prognostic analyses were univariate because of sparse events, leaving substantial potential for residual confounding.
Neurologic outcomes were recorded as a binary residual-deficit measure without systematic severity grading.
Diagnostic methods changed over the 45-year period, specimen timing was unavailable, and missing data limited comparisons of culture and molecular-test performance.
Treatment was nonrandomized, adjunctive gentamicin duration varied, and confounding by indication could affect treatment-outcome associations.
The long study period spanned major changes in diagnostics, antimicrobial management, and supportive care, complicating temporal comparisons.
One-year all-cause mortality may include deaths related to comorbidity rather than invasive listeriosis itself.
The authors reported no funding for the study.
The authors declared no conflicts of interest.
The authors stated that underlying data are included in the article and its supplementary material.
